1013.bp: Imagine a user who has one collection of images from one visual world and wants to find matching images in another visual world. The same object or scene may be present in both places, but the surface appearance can change: source, style, lighting, composition, or collection habits may differ enough that a machine sees two separate worlds. This paper serves cross-domain image retrieval, where the goal is not merely to find visually similar pixels, but to retrieve images that carry the same semantic content across a domain gap. The hard practical case is that neither side comes with annotations, so there are no trusted category labels or paired examples saying which image in one domain corresponds to which image in the other. The paper asks how a retrieval system can build a shared sense of meaning when it cannot rely on human labels, and when self-made clues from the two image collections may be unstable.
1013.wh: The central difficulty is that the system must learn two things at once: what each image means and how meanings should line up across domains. If it only studies one collection internally, it may find groups that are locally coherent, such as images that look alike inside that collection. But a local group is not automatically a category that transfers. The other domain may represent the same category with different textures, backgrounds, colors, or image styles. Existing unsupervised methods derive supervision signals from the data itself, meaning they manufacture their own hints about which images should be close. That can help, but it also creates a ceiling: if the internal hints are wrong or incomplete, the model keeps reinforcing its own uncertain guesses. Without stable semantic references, category-level correspondence across domains can drift, so the retrieval system may confidently align the wrong clusters.
1013.naive: A smart beginner would first compare images by ordinary visual similarity, then return the nearest images from the other domain. If that fails, the beginner might cluster each domain separately and try to align clusters that seem similar. Both ideas break for the same reason: appearance and meaning are not the same thing. Two images of the same category can look far apart when they come from different domains, while two images from different categories can look close because they share color, texture, or composition. Clustering each domain separately also gives no guarantee that cluster one in domain A means the same thing as cluster one in domain B. The method needs guidance that is less trapped inside either collection.
1013.ap: The paper's central move is to borrow a stable outside judge before training the retrieval model. A pre-trained foundation model, already exposed to broad visual concepts, is used as external semantic guidance. The method then builds a dual-scope constraint bank: a store of high-confidence positive and negative relations both within a domain and across domains. A positive relation says two images should be treated as semantically close; a negative relation says they should be kept apart. The word selective matters because the system does not trust every possible pair. It keeps the relations that the outside model marks with high confidence, using them as firmer anchors than internally induced clues alone. Training then uses these constraints to pull related images together, push unrelated images apart, align the two domains, and preserve stable structure inside each domain through prototype-centered forces.
1013.mech: The inputs are two unlabeled image collections from different domains and the images that must later be retrieved across those domains. First, each image is passed through a pre-trained foundation model to obtain semantic evidence about what other images it appears to match or not match. The method does not turn all pairwise guesses into training truth. It selects high-confidence positive and negative relations and stores them in a dual-scope constraint bank. One scope concerns relations within a single domain, which helps keep images of the same apparent category compact inside that domain. The other scope concerns relations across domains, which gives the model bridges between visually different collections. During learning, the retrieval model is trained with a generic constraint loss. In plain terms, the loss defines what counts as wrong: positives being too far apart is wrong, negatives being too close is wrong, and poor cross-domain alignment is wrong. The model changes its internal image descriptions to reduce those errors. A second pressure, prototypical geometry regularization, treats category-like centers as anchors. Images are pulled toward suitable prototypes and pushed away from unsuitable ones, so each domain keeps a stable internal shape while the two domains become comparable. The output is a retrieval representation in which an image from one domain can search for semantically consistent images in the other.
1013.math: The main mathematical idea is similarity as controlled nearness. Each image is represented by numbers that let the system compare images, but the important question is who teaches the numbers what nearness should mean. If nearness is learned only from one collection's own patterns, it may preserve style instead of category. SCL changes the training pressure by adding constraints: chosen pairs must be nearer or farther according to high-confidence semantic relations. This is learning by comparison of similar and different cases. The constraint loss is an error measure that penalizes the wrong geometry, such as a positive pair landing far apart or a negative pair landing close together. The optimization, meaning the repeated adjustment of model settings to reduce that error, is guided by those selected relations. Prototypes add another geometric idea: instead of every image floating independently, the method uses representative centers and pull-and-push forces around them. Pulling creates compactness within a domain, so related images do not scatter. Pushing protects separation, so unlike categories do not collapse together. The tradeoff is external guidance versus selectivity: outside semantic knowledge can anchor the task, but only if the chosen constraints are reliable enough not to import confident mistakes.
1013.dots: This paper sits at the meeting point of retrieval, similarity learning, and unsupervised domain adaptation. Like other retrieval papers, it is ultimately about choosing useful candidates from a large pile, but its query and target live in different visual worlds. Like the broader similarity family in the repo, it turns messy objects into a map where closeness is supposed to mean task-relevant sameness. The special pressure here is false sameness across domains: surface likeness may be misleading, and local clusters may not transfer. It also connects to self-supervised and comparison-based learning, because the method creates training signal from positive and negative relations rather than from human labels. Compared with ranking papers, this work focuses more on building the comparison surface before ranking candidates. Once that surface is better aligned, ordinary retrieval ranking has a more meaningful distance or score to sort by.
1013.ww: The method should improve over the naive approach because it separates two jobs that unsupervised retrieval often entangles. The first job is finding semantic anchors, and the second is training a domain-aligned retrieval model. If the model invents all anchors from the same unlabeled data it is trying to align, early mistakes can become training instructions. By using a pre-trained foundation model as an external semantic prior, SCL starts with signals that are less dependent on either target domain's local quirks. The selective constraint bank then reduces noise by keeping high-confidence positives and negatives instead of treating every guessed relation as equally useful. Positive constraints create bridges for images that should match within or across domains. Negative constraints stop broad alignment from merging different categories just because domains need to be brought together. Prototypical geometry regularization adds stability: it asks each domain to remain internally organized around representative centers while cross-domain relations are learned. That combination fits the problem because successful retrieval needs both alignment across domains and separation inside each domain.
1013.po: The payoff is a cross-domain image retrieval system that can search for semantically consistent images without annotations in either domain. The abstract reports extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks and says SCL consistently outperforms prior methods, so the claimed gain is better retrieval accuracy when domain gaps are large. Practically, the capability is useful wherever image collections come from different sources or styles and manual labeling is too costly. The paper's contribution is not just another matching rule; it is a way to inject stable external semantic guidance while still learning the structure needed for the particular unlabeled domains.
1013.limits: The method assumes the pre-trained foundation model provides useful semantic judgments for the domains being searched. If that outside model is weak on the image types, biased toward the wrong visual cues, or confidently wrong, the constraint bank can anchor the retrieval model to bad relations. The abstract also does not specify how confidence thresholds behave across all domain gaps, or how sensitive the result is to prototype quality. Benchmark success supports the claim, but it does not prove the method will work for every specialized image collection. The approach also depends on the selected positives and negatives being rich enough to cover categories rather than only easy examples.

1014.bp: A search system is useful only if the few results shown first answer the user's need better than the thousands left below. To improve that ordering, engineers need judgments about which documents are relevant. Human judgments are costly, so large language models, text systems trained to read and generate language, are now used as cheaper judges. This paper asks a more practical question than whether those judges can score systems: can their judgments become fuel for making the search system itself better? The paper focuses on multi-criteria relevance labels. Instead of asking for one relevance score, the judge separates relevance into Exactness, Coverage, Topicality, and Contextual Fit. That matters because a document can mention the right topic while failing to answer the exact need, or answer one part while missing the surrounding context. The real-world goal is a reranker that learns from these finer reasons, not just from a single retrieval score.
1014.wh: The hard part is that relevance is not one clean property. A document can be topically related to the query, cover many aspects of the issue, fit the user's situation, and still fail to be the exact answer. Traditional ranking features often compress all of this into a retrieval score, which is convenient but blunt. LLM-judge grades are richer, but they arrive from an evaluator whose usual job is comparison: decide whether system A did better than system B. Turning those grades into training features raises several tensions. The grades may overlap with existing retrieval scores, so they might add little. They may help weak systems because weak systems miss obvious relevance cues, but matter less for strong systems whose retrieval scores already capture much of the signal. They may also depend on the dataset. The paper therefore has to show not only that multi-criteria labels correlate with relevance, but that they add usable information for learning to rank.
1014.naive: A smart beginner would take the search engine's original retrieval score and sort documents from highest to lowest. If automated judging is available, the beginner might ask the LLM judge for one overall relevance grade and use that grade as a replacement score. That fails for two reasons. First, the original score and one overall grade both hide the reason a document is useful. A result might be weak in coverage but strong in contextual fit, and a single number cannot show that distinction. Second, replacing the retrieval score assumes the judge is always better than the search system. The abstract suggests the relationship changes with system quality: weaker systems benefit most from the judge grades, while stronger systems still need their retrieval scores.
1014.ap: The paper's core idea is to stop treating LLM-based evaluation as the end of the process. Instead, it turns each criterion grade into a separate input feature for a learning-to-rank model. Learning to rank means training a model to sort candidate documents by using examples of better and worse orderings. Here, the candidates still have retrieval scores, but they also receive LLM-judge descriptions of why they match: Exactness, Coverage, Topicality, and Contextual Fit. The ranker can then learn how much each reason should matter for the final order. The authors test this against manual relevance labels from TREC DL 2019, DL 2020, and DL 2023. They also examine feature importance, asking whether the judge-derived criteria matter more or less than retrieval scores as the underlying IR system becomes stronger.
1014.mech: The mechanism starts with a query and a set of candidate search results produced by an information retrieval system. Each query-document pair has the system's own retrieval score, which is the system's current estimate of usefulness. The paper then adds another layer of evidence: a multi-criteria LLM judge reads the pair and assigns grades along four named dimensions. Exactness asks whether the document directly answers the query. Coverage asks whether it includes the needed aspects rather than only a fragment. Topicality asks whether it is about the same subject. Contextual Fit asks whether the document fits the situation implied by the query, not merely the words. These grades are not collapsed into one score. They are passed as separate features into a learning-to-rank model, along with the retrieval score. The ranker is trained and evaluated using manual relevance labels from TREC DL 2019, DL 2020, and DL 2023, so the final target is still human relevance judgment. During analysis, the authors compare how much the learned model relies on each judge criterion versus the original retrieval score across retrieval systems of different quality. The output is a reranked result list, measured by NDCG@20, a ranking metric that rewards placing highly relevant documents near the top twenty positions.
1014.math: The central mathematical idea is ranking: choosing an order when only a few items can be shown and mistakes near the top are especially costly. A ranking model needs features, which are measured clues about each query-document pair, and a training target, which tells it what a better order looks like. In this paper, the clues include the old retrieval score and four LLM-judge grades. The training target comes from manual relevance labels. The model's job is to learn a rule for combining the clues so that documents judged more relevant move upward. This is an optimization problem in plain terms: define wrongness as putting useful results too low, then adjust the combination of features to reduce that wrongness on labeled examples. The multi-criteria grades also use decomposition. Instead of asking whether relevance exists, they split relevance into several observable reasons. That split is mathematically useful because it gives the ranker more axes on which two documents can differ. Feature importance is another scoring idea: after training, ask which inputs changed the ranking decisions most. The abstract's key finding is that Contextual Fit often becomes the main discriminator, while retrieval score dominates as system quality rises.
1014.dots: This paper sits in the repo's information retrieval and search thread because it studies the basic search pressure: how to choose the best few documents from a much larger pile. It connects to the neighboring unbiased learning-to-rank paper in the same batch, which asks whether click data can really separate relevance from position bias. Both papers worry that a ranking model can learn the wrong lesson if its evidence is incomplete or misleading. It also connects to document screening stopping, where ranking quality changes the cost of what a human must inspect next. A better top order can save review effort. The LLM connection is specific: the model is not generating an answer or using tools; it is supplying structured judgments that become features. That places the paper near broader 2026 work that turns language-model outputs into supervision for retrieval, recommendation, and evaluation rather than treating them as final products.
1014.ww: The approach can work because different relevance failures leave different traces. A document that is topical but not exact should not be treated the same as a document that is exact but incomplete. A single retrieval score can blur those cases because it must summarize all evidence into one number. Multi-criteria grades preserve the separate reasons long enough for the ranker to learn their relative value. This matters most for weaker retrieval systems because their original scores leave more room for an outside judge to correct coarse mistakes. The abstract reports exactly that pattern: weaker IR systems benefit the most. Contextual Fit becoming a primary discriminator is also intuitive. Many bad search results share query words and even cover the broad topic, but fail because they do not match the user's intended situation. As systems become stronger, their retrieval scores already encode more relevance signal, so the LLM-judge grades shift from being the main guide to being a complementary source that helps in dataset-dependent cases.
1014.po: The payoff is a way to make LLM-based evaluation productive rather than merely diagnostic. The abstract reports 14% to 36% improvements in NDCG@20 across diverse IR systems, with the largest gains for weaker systems. Practically, this means a search team could use multi-criteria LLM-judge labeling to create training features for reranking, then still validate against manual TREC relevance labels. The paper also buys interpretability of a limited kind: feature-importance analysis can show whether the reranker relied on Exactness, Coverage, Topicality, Contextual Fit, or the original retrieval score.
1014.limits: The result depends on the LLM judge producing grades that are reliable enough to help rather than inject bias. The abstract evaluates against TREC DL 2019, DL 2020, and DL 2023, but it does not prove the same criteria will help every search domain, language, query type, or collection. The method also assumes the four criteria are the right decomposition of relevance; other tasks may need freshness, authority, safety, or diversity. The gains are reported for reranking and NDCG@20, so the abstract does not establish latency cost, deployment stability, user satisfaction, or whether repeated training on judge labels could amplify the judge's systematic mistakes.

1015.bp: A recommendation catalog is not a fixed library. New products, songs, videos, or posts arrive, and old ones change meaning as people start using them in different company. This paper is about generative recommendation, where the system recommends by writing an item identifier as a short sequence of discrete code pieces, much as a writing model predicts the next piece of text. A separate mapper first turns each item into that code, and the recommender learns to predict codes from user histories. The useful trick is that items with similar user behavior can receive similar codes, so the recommender can share evidence across related items. The hard part is time. If a new item needs a code, or if an old item's neighborhood of co-clicks and co-purchases changes, the code system must adapt without erasing what the recommender already learned about the old codes.
1015.wh: The central tension is stability versus plasticity. Plasticity means the code maker must be willing to change when the catalog and user behavior change. Stability means most old item codes should remain recognizable to the recommender, because the recommender has already attached learned numeric meaning to those code pieces. New items create code collisions and shifts: two items can want the same identifier, or the arrival of one item can force nearby codes to move. New interactions create collaborative drift, meaning an existing item's behavioral companions, popularity, or co-occurrence pattern no longer look the same. Fully retraining both the code maker and the recommender can handle the new world, but the abstract says that cost is often too high. Simply fine-tuning the code maker is also dangerous, because it may change the token sequences for many existing items and break the recommender's learned alignment between old codes and item meaning.
1015.naive: A smart beginner might update the item-code maker whenever fresh interactions arrive, then keep using the existing recommender with the new codes. That sounds efficient because only one component changes. But the recommender has learned that a particular code sequence points toward a particular region of user preference. If fine-tuning changes many old code sequences, the recommender is suddenly reading familiar items under unfamiliar names. Another beginner might freeze all old codes and assign only new ones, but then truly drifting items keep stale identifiers. The system would preserve old knowledge at the cost of missing real changes in user behavior.
1015.ap: DACT's core move is to stop treating every item as equally changed. It adds a Collaborative Drift Identification Module, a learned detector that gives each item a drift confidence: a score for how likely that item's behavior-based meaning has moved. During tokenizer fine-tuning, items judged to be drifting and items judged to be stationary receive different treatment, so the system can learn from changed evidence without shaking the whole catalog. After that, DACT reassigns codes hierarchically through a relaxed-to-strict process. In plain terms, it first allows more flexible code movement to find plausible new homes, then tightens the rules so unnecessary changes are limited. The paper is therefore not only updating codes; it is deciding which codes deserve to move, how far they should move, and when the old code structure should be protected.
1015.mech: The input is a stream-like recommendation setting: an existing item-code mapper, an existing generative recommender that predicts those code sequences, old item-interaction patterns, new items, and new interactions. First, the tokenizer is fine-tuned rather than rebuilt from scratch. During this update, CDIM is trained jointly with it. CDIM looks at item-level collaborative evidence, meaning the pattern of users and other items that surround an item through behavior, and outputs a drift confidence. The abstract does not give the detector's exact features, so the supported claim is that it estimates drift from collaborative change, not from side information such as text or images. Second, the fine-tuning objective treats drifting and stationary items differently. Drifting items need freedom to change their identifiers, while stationary items need pressure to keep their old identifiers so the recommender can still read them. Third, after the tokenizer update, DACT performs hierarchical code reassignment. Hierarchical means the identifier has multiple positions or levels, and reassignment can be controlled level by level rather than as one all-or-nothing name swap. The relaxed-to-strict strategy begins with looser matching so changed items can find better codes, then applies stricter constraints to avoid needless churn. The output is an updated set of item code sequences intended to fit the evolved catalog while disturbing as few stable items as possible.
1015.math: The first mathematical idea is representation by discrete sequences: each item is compressed into a short code made of separate symbols. The tradeoff is compression versus detail. A short code is efficient and can make related items share structure, but it can also collide or become stale when the catalog changes. The second idea is similarity from behavior. Two items are considered near when users interact with them in similar patterns; this is useful because recommendations depend on collective behavior, but it can mislead when popularity or co-occurrence shifts for reasons that are temporary or external. The third idea is optimization, which here means defining what counts as wrong and adjusting the tokenizer to reduce that wrongness. DACT changes the usual objective by weighting items according to drift confidence, so the system is not punished in the same way for moving a genuinely changed item as for moving a stable one. The fourth idea is constrained reassignment. Code choices are not free labels; they must preserve enough old alignment for the recommender. The relaxed-to-strict schedule is a way of searching broadly first and then narrowing the allowed changes, balancing adaptation against disruption.
1015.dots: This paper sits inside generative recommendation, but its deeper problem is shared with many conference papers about systems that must keep learning after deployment. It connects to recommendation work on cold-start items because both ask how a model should absorb new catalog objects without waiting for full retraining. It also connects to dynamic recommendation and continual learning, where new behavior carries useful signal but can make a model forget older regularities. The recurring mathematical shape is selective updating: change the parts whose evidence has moved, and preserve the parts whose old meaning is still useful. It also touches ranking and retrieval because item codes are not merely storage names; they determine what the recommender can generate and therefore what items can appear near the top. The paper's specific contribution is to apply this stability-adaptation tradeoff to collaborative tokenizers, where behavior-shaped codes are valuable precisely because they are also vulnerable to behavioral drift.
1015.ww: The method should help because most real change is uneven. In a large catalog, some items are genuinely changing because new competitors arrive, user tastes move, or popularity patterns shift. Many other items are probably stable enough that their old codes still serve the recommender well. A uniform update wastes effort on the stable group and creates unnecessary breakage. By estimating item-level drift, DACT gives the update process a rough map of where change is needed. That protects the recommender's learned code-to-meaning alignment for stationary items while giving drifting items room to receive better identifiers. The hierarchical reassignment adds another source of control. If a code has several levels, a system can adjust coarse and fine parts differently instead of replacing the whole identifier abruptly. The relaxed-to-strict schedule also matches the problem's shape: early looseness lets the system explore changed code assignments, while later strictness prevents the exploration from turning into catalog-wide code churn. The improvement comes from reducing two errors at once: stale codes for changed items and unnecessary code changes for stable items.
1015.po: The payoff is a recommendation updater that is cheaper and less disruptive than retraining both the tokenizer and the generative recommender from scratch. According to the abstract, experiments on three real-world datasets and two representative generative recommender models show that DACT performs better than baselines. The practical capability is continual catalog maintenance: new items can be incorporated, and old items whose collaborative meaning has drifted can be adjusted, while prior knowledge is less likely to be destroyed. For a live recommender, that means fresher suggestions without treating every catalog update as a full rebuild.
1015.limits: The abstract leaves several assumptions open. DACT depends on drift confidence being meaningful; if CDIM mistakes a stable item for a drifting one, the system may still make unnecessary code changes, and if it misses real drift, stale identifiers remain. The approach also assumes collaborative behavior is available and informative enough to detect change. Sparse new items or noisy interaction bursts may make that hard. The abstract reports three datasets and two recommender models, but does not prove behavior under every catalog size, update frequency, or deployment cost. It also does not show from the excerpt exactly how drift confidence is calibrated or how much code movement is acceptable before alignment breaks.

1016.bp: Start with a professional searcher facing a long ranked list of documents. A patent examiner is looking for earlier inventions that may decide whether a new patent should be granted. A medical reviewer is looking for studies that may decide what evidence enters a systematic review. In both cases, search is not finished when the system returns results. A person still has to inspect documents one by one and eventually decide that reading more is no longer worth it. That stopping decision is the real object of the paper. Stopping too early can miss a document that matters for law, medicine, or scientific evidence. Stopping too late spends expert time on documents whose chance of changing the final decision is small. The paper asks for a stopping rule that respects the purpose of the search. Instead of treating every task as a race toward the same recall target, it asks what each extra document is expected to buy.
1016.wh: The hard part is that the searcher does not know what remains unseen. If all relevant documents were already labeled, stopping would be easy. The searcher could count what was found, count what was missed, and choose perfectly. Real screening is different: after reviewing the top part of the list, the searcher only sees the documents already examined and whatever evidence the ranking system provides about the rest. Existing Technology-Assisted Review stopping rules try to hit a pre-specified recall target, meaning a chosen fraction of all relevant documents. That sounds objective, but it hides the reason for the task. Missing one patent document may be much more costly than reading ten extra candidates. In another review setting, the cost of more screening may dominate once the likely remaining value is low. The difficulty is therefore not only estimating relevance. It is comparing two unlike things: the uncertain benefit of finding more relevant material and the concrete cost of continuing to read.
1016.naive: A smart beginner would choose a fixed target such as stop when we think we have found 95 percent of the relevant documents. This is appealing because it turns stopping into a clean counting problem. It fails because the same percentage can mean different practical consequences in different jobs. Another beginner might stop after the search scores become low or after a long run of nonrelevant documents. That also fails because low score is not the same as low value. If the next relevant document would strongly change a patent or medical conclusion, even a small chance may justify continuing. If the payoff is modest and review time is expensive, the same chance may not. A task-blind rule cannot price these consequences.
1016.ap: The paper's core idea is to turn stopping into a decision problem. A decision problem begins by naming the available actions, the uncertain facts, and the costs and rewards attached to outcomes. Here the action is simple: review more results or stop now. The uncertain fact is whether unseen documents still contain relevant evidence worth finding. The cost is the effort of examining additional documents. The reward, or avoided loss, is the value of finding relevant material that would otherwise be missed. The paper uses Expected Value of Perfect Information, which asks a plain question: how much would it be worth to know the hidden answer before acting? If perfect knowledge about the remaining documents would not be worth the cost of acquiring more evidence, stopping is reasonable. From this idea, the authors derive three practical stopping policies and test them on patent examining and medical systematic review tasks.
1016.mech: The mechanism begins with a screened search result list for a professional task. Some documents have already been reviewed, so the system has evidence about how many useful documents have appeared and how the ranked list is behaving. The task also supplies a cost and payoff setting: reading another document consumes expert effort, while discovering a relevant document produces value or avoids harm. The method then considers the choice at the current point in the review. Stopping gives an immediate saving in review effort but risks leaving relevant documents unseen. Continuing buys more information, because the next reviewed documents reveal whether useful evidence remains. The Expected Value of Perfect Information step imagines the best possible version of that uncertainty: if the searcher could know the hidden relevance status of remaining material before deciding, how much better could the decision become? That value becomes a measuring stick for whether further review is worth buying. The paper derives three stopping policies from this decision-theoretic view, so the exact rule can be made practical rather than requiring impossible perfect knowledge. Each policy estimates whether the expected gain from more screening exceeds the expected cost under the current task's assumptions. The output is a recommendation to stop or continue. In experiments, those recommendations are judged not only by recall but by net utility, meaning the final balance of benefits and costs under the evaluated settings.
1016.math: The main mathematical idea is decision theory: a way to choose among actions when each action has uncertain consequences. It does not ask only what is most likely. It asks what each possible outcome is worth or costs. In this paper, the actions are stop and continue, the uncertain state is the relevance of unseen documents, and the score is net utility, the benefit left after subtracting costs. A second idea is expected value. Expected value means averaging possible outcomes after weighting them by how likely they are. If there is a small chance of a very valuable document, that chance can still matter; if the chance is tiny and review cost is high, it may not. A third idea is the value of information. Information has value when learning it can change the action a rational searcher would take. Perfect information is an idealized upper bound: it asks what the decision would be worth if uncertainty disappeared. The paper uses that ideal to derive practical stopping policies. This math fits because screening is a sequential choice under partial sight. The central tradeoff is recall versus effort, but the paper makes that tradeoff task-specific instead of pretending one recall target has the same meaning everywhere.
1016.dots: In the repo's broader map, this paper sits inside information retrieval and search, but it shifts attention from ranking documents to deciding when enough evidence has been gathered. It connects to ranking because the reviewed documents arrive in an order created by a search system, and errors near the top or near the stopping boundary matter more than errors buried far below. It connects to probability because the searcher must estimate what may remain unseen from partial evidence. It connects to optimization in the plain sense of choosing an action that improves a stated score: continue only when the likely value justifies the cost. It also sits near evaluation work because the abstract judges methods by net utility rather than by relevance alone. Neighboring retrieval papers ask which documents to retrieve, how to order them, or how much context to pass forward. This paper asks the next operational question: once documents are being screened by people, when should the process end?
1016.ww: The approach should work better than a fixed recall rule because it measures the thing the user actually cares about. Recall treats every missed relevant document as the same kind of error and every extra reviewed document as outside the main target. Professional screening does not work that way. The point of reading is to support a downstream decision, and the cost of reading is paid by scarce expert labor. By putting both sides into the same decision calculation, the method can recommend longer review when the remaining possible evidence is valuable enough and earlier stopping when further evidence is unlikely to repay its cost. Expected Value of Perfect Information is useful because it gives a disciplined way to ask whether uncertainty is worth reducing. If even perfect knowledge would add little value, then spending more effort to reduce uncertainty is hard to justify. If hidden documents could change the decision enough, continued review remains worthwhile. The paper's experiments support this logic by showing higher net utility than existing stopping methods under the evaluated cost and payoff settings.
1016.po: The payoff is a stopping decision that is tied to the professional purpose of screening. The abstract reports experiments on CLEF-IP patent data and medical systematic review datasets. Under the evaluated cost and payoff settings, the decision-theoretic policies generally produce more appropriate stopping decisions than existing methods, shown by higher net utility. The practical capability is not merely finding more relevant documents. It is knowing when extra review is no longer worth the expert effort for the task at hand. That can save time when continuing has low value and protect quality when missing documents would be costly.
1016.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The cost and payoff settings must reflect the real task; if they are wrong, the stopping rule can faithfully optimize the wrong tradeoff. The method also depends on the evidence available during screening being informative about unseen documents. If the ranking system is badly calibrated, if relevant documents are scattered unpredictably, or if the datasets differ from the deployment setting, the expected values may mislead. The abstract reports results on patent examining and systematic review datasets, but it does not prove the same behavior for every domain, every review protocol, or every way of valuing missed evidence. It also does not specify from the abstract alone how users should choose the costs and payoffs in contested real cases.

1017.bp: Search engines learn from clicks because clicks are abundant and cheap. But a click is not a clean statement that a document was the best answer. A result near the top is more likely to be seen, and therefore more likely to be clicked, even when a lower result is equally relevant or better. Unbiased learning to rank tries to repair that measurement problem: it wants to learn the document's real usefulness while separating away the extra lift caused by position on the page. This paper asks a prior question that is easy to ignore: can the data actually support that separation? In a two-tower model, one side represents relevance and another represents position bias. The promise is that clicks can teach both. The danger is that the same clicks may be explainable by many different mixtures of relevance and position bias.
1017.wh: The hard part is that relevance and position bias are tangled in the same observed event. A user either clicked or did not click; the log does not directly say whether the click happened because the document answered the query or because it appeared in an easy-to-see slot. If the same document, or a document with similar features, appears in many different positions, the system gets a useful comparison: what changes when position changes but the document is roughly the same? Existing theory says this can identify the two parts in the limit of endless data. Real logs are less generous. Some documents rarely move positions, some features do not overlap across positions, and sample sizes can be small for particular parameters. Then a model may fit clicks well while still leaving some bias parameters free to drift without being pinned down by evidence.
1017.naive: A smart beginner would train the two-tower ranking model, check whether click prediction is accurate, and assume the learned relevance and position-bias values are trustworthy. That fails because good prediction does not guarantee unique explanation. Two different settings can predict the same clicks: one can say the top position is very attractive and the document is only moderately relevant; another can say the top position matters less and the document is very relevant. If both stories fit the observed clicks, the model has not really learned the separate causes. It has only found one convenient explanation among several equally plausible ones.
1017.ap: The paper's central move is to turn identifiability into a practical stress test. Instead of asking only whether a trained model predicts clicks, it asks whether each individual bias parameter is forced by the data. The diagnostic takes a parameter at its best learned value, deliberately shifts it away, retrains the parts of the model that are allowed to compensate, and checks whether click-prediction performance gets meaningfully worse. If performance drops, the data objected to that shift; the parameter was constrained. If performance barely changes, the model found another way to explain the clicks, so that parameter was not uniquely determined. This changes identifiability from an infinite-data theorem into an empirical question about the actual log, logging policy, feature overlap, and sample size in front of the practitioner.
1017.mech: The mechanism starts with a click dataset from a ranking system. Each record carries the displayed document, its position, and whether the user clicked. A two-tower model is trained to explain those clicks by combining a relevance part, tied to query-document information, with a position-bias part, tied to where the result appeared. After fitting the model, the diagnostic selects one bias parameter, such as the parameter for a particular position. It moves that parameter away from the value found during training. The rest of the model is then retrained or adjusted so it has a fair chance to recover click-prediction performance under the forced change. The diagnostic compares the new prediction loss with the original loss. A clear loss increase means the data could not absorb the artificial shift; that parameter is identified in the practical sense tested here. A flat loss curve means the model can compensate elsewhere, so the parameter is not pinned down. Repeating this for individual bias parameters builds a map of which parts of the bias model are supported. Simulations then vary logging randomness, feature overlap, and sample size to separate structural failures from failures caused by too little data.
1017.math: The central mathematical idea is identifiability, which means uniqueness of explanation. If a clock shows noon, many hidden mechanisms could have produced that reading unless the observations rule all but one out. Here the visible reading is the click log, and the hidden mechanisms are relevance and position bias. A parameter is identifiable when changing it necessarily worsens the model's ability to account for the observed clicks after every allowed adjustment elsewhere. The second idea is loss minimization, which means defining a number that counts prediction error and choosing model settings that make that number small. The diagnostic studies the shape of that error number around a parameter. If the error rises when the parameter is moved, the data creates a valley with a real bottom. If the error stays nearly flat, the parameter lies on a plateau where many settings explain the clicks equally well. The paper also uses comparison logic: same or similar documents appearing across positions create the contrast needed to separate document appeal from position advantage. The tradeoff is reliability versus convenience: a model can be convenient to fit while its internal parts remain underdetermined.
1017.dots: This paper sits inside information retrieval and search, but its deeper theme is separating cause from coincidence in logged behavior. Click logs are also used by recommendation, advertising, and personalization systems, and all face the same danger: observed action is shaped by both user preference and the platform's previous decision about what to show. It also connects to ranking because the learned model is not merely predicting clicks; it is supposed to produce a better ordering of documents once position effects are removed. The diagnostic resembles broader conference ideas about testing whether a learned score is actually constrained by evidence rather than just tuned to a dataset. Neighboring two-tower papers often focus on speed and matching quality. This one focuses on trust: before using a fast architecture to correct bias, ask whether the data contains enough variation for the correction to mean anything.
1017.ww: The diagnostic works because unidentified parameters have a distinctive behavior: they can move without changing what the model says about the observed clicks. If the data never shows enough variation to distinguish two explanations, retraining can hide a forced change by adjusting other parts of the model. That is not a small numerical accident; it is evidence that the dataset does not contain the comparison needed to decide. Identified parameters behave differently. Their values are tied to actual contrasts in the log, such as documents or similar feature patterns appearing at different positions. When such a parameter is shifted, the model loses an explanation that the other parts cannot fully replace, so prediction error rises. The test is useful because it measures sensitivity in the finite dataset instead of assuming endless examples. It can also distinguish several failure sources: a modeling assumption may be wrong, the logging policy may not move documents enough, or there may simply be too few samples to expose the constraint.
1017.po: The payoff is a diagnostic tool for practitioners who use two-tower models to correct position bias in learning to rank. It tells them which bias parameters are actually determined by their data and which can vary without hurting click prediction. The abstract reports simulations showing how non-deterministic logging policies, feature overlap, and larger samples affect identifiability. It also reports a real-world application to Baidu-ULTR where some parameters remain unidentified despite large click data. The practical benefit is avoiding false confidence: a system can predict clicks while still failing to learn the bias correction it claims to learn.
1017.limits: The method assumes that prediction loss is a meaningful test of whether a shifted parameter has damaged the model's explanation of clicks. It also depends on how retraining is done after a shift; if the retraining procedure is weak, a parameter might look identified because the model failed to compensate. The abstract establishes simulations and one real dataset application, but it does not prove that every logging environment, query mix, or two-tower design will behave the same way. The diagnostic can reveal that a parameter is not pinned down; by itself, it does not create the missing positional variation or prove that learned relevance is correct.

1018.bp: Search systems often need two different skills. One skill is broad meaning: knowing that two differently worded passages may answer the same need. The other is exact matching: keeping a visible list of important words so a fast search engine can match query terms to document terms. Learned sparse retrieval tries to combine those skills. It lets a language model decide which vocabulary entries should represent a query or document, but the final object is still sparse: most vocabulary entries are zero, and only a few terms carry weight. This paper starts from a surprising practical failure. Modern encoders such as ModernBERT are stronger in dense retrieval, where meaning is compared through compact learned descriptions, yet they can trail old BERT-base in learned sparse retrieval. The paper argues that the failure is not that the newer models understand language worse. Their word inventory was built for faithful text reconstruction, not for sparse matching.
1018.wh: Sparse retrieval is hard because it asks a model to be selective with words. The model must keep terms that help matching and avoid spending its limited output positions on spelling, case, and small surface variants that do not change the search meaning. A raw, case-sensitive vocabulary is useful when the job is to rebuild the original text exactly, because uppercase letters, suffixes, and rare forms matter. But retrieval has a different pressure. If one semantic unit is split across many redundant surface forms, the model must learn many nearly repeated ways to express the same match. That wastes capacity and makes lexical matching less reliable. The abstract calls this the Vocabulary Gap: modern tokenizers map single meanings to redundant forms, creating morphological noise. The difficulty is that simply shrinking the vocabulary is risky. If the coarse vocabulary merges words that should stay distinct, the system may gain simplicity while losing meaning.
1018.naive: A smart beginner would take a modern encoder, keep its existing vocabulary, and fine-tune it for learned sparse retrieval. That seems natural because the same encoder already performs well when retrieval is done with dense learned descriptions. The beginner might expect the training process to learn which terms matter and ignore redundant ones. According to the abstract, standard fine-tuning does not solve the mismatch. The model is still tied to a raw vocabulary designed for lossless reconstruction, so sparse matching must spread evidence across repeated surface forms. Another beginner fix would be to replace the vocabulary with a normalized one directly. That can also fail because the pretrained model's learned word relationships may be disrupted, causing inactive outputs or collapse into overly dense behavior.
1018.ap: The central move is to transfer the modern encoder into a vocabulary that behaves better for sparse retrieval without throwing away what the encoder already learned. The paper calls this Vocabulary Transfer. Instead of treating the vocabulary as a fixed engineering detail, it treats the vocabulary as part of the model's search language. The method moves the encoder from a raw, case-sensitive inventory toward a sparse-friendly normalized inventory, where related surface forms can be grouped when their meaning should remain intact. The transfer is meant to be model-agnostic, so it is not only a special repair for ModernBERT. Two mechanisms protect the move. Semantic Initialization via spatial topology tries to preserve the old geometry: words or pieces that were near each other in the learned organization should not be scattered randomly after transfer. Activation Potential Calibration then aligns the pretrained model's internal signals with the sparse output constraint.
1018.mech: The input is a pretrained encoder, such as ModernBERT, whose vocabulary was built to represent text faithfully, including raw case-sensitive forms. The desired output is a learned sparse retriever: for a query or document, the model should activate only a small number of useful vocabulary entries and assign them weights for matching. The mechanism first identifies that the old vocabulary contains redundant surface forms for the same semantic unit. It then chooses a coarser, normalized vocabulary that is more suitable for lexical matching, while preserving semantic integrity so that distinct meanings are not carelessly merged. Vocabulary Transfer migrates the encoder to that new vocabulary. Semantic Initialization uses the spatial topology of the pretrained model's learned organization, meaning the pattern of which terms sit near or relate to which others, to initialize the new vocabulary entries. This avoids starting the new sparse vocabulary from arbitrary positions. Then Activation Potential Calibration adjusts how strongly the model's internal features can activate output terms under sparsity constraints. That matters because ordinary fine-tuning can create dead neurons, where useful output units rarely fire, or dense collapse, where too many entries fire and the result stops being sparse. The final system emits sparse term-weight vectors that can be used by efficient lexical retrieval while carrying knowledge from the modern encoder.
1018.math: The main mathematical idea is controlled compression. The vocabulary is a set of possible symbols the model may use to describe queries and documents. A raw vocabulary has many symbols that differ on the page but play almost the same role for retrieval. Coarse-graining means replacing several fine distinctions with a broader unit when those distinctions do not help the task. This can reduce the size and complexity of the hypothesis class, which is the family of patterns the model is allowed to learn. A smaller family is easier to learn from finite data because there are fewer accidental rules that fit the training examples but fail later. That is what the abstract means by tighter generalization bounds. The condition is semantic integrity: compression is helpful only if the merged forms really should share evidence. The second mathematical object is geometry, the learned arrangement in which related terms or features have meaningful neighborhoods. Semantic Initialization tries to preserve that neighborhood structure during transfer. The third idea is sparse activation: most output weights should be zero, so matching remains efficient and interpretable. Calibration tunes the threshold-like behavior between silence and activation, balancing too little signal against too much dense noise.
1018.dots: This paper sits inside the information-retrieval family because it repairs a basic search failure: choosing a small useful set of terms from a huge vocabulary so documents can be matched and ranked. It connects to similarity because the encoder already has a learned organization of terms and meanings, and Vocabulary Transfer tries to keep that neighborhood structure while changing the vocabulary. It connects to ranking because sparse retrieval ultimately gives weighted terms that help order documents for a query; bad vocabulary choices can push relevant documents down by splitting the same evidence across variants. It also sits next to efficiency work in sparse retrieval, such as local batch papers about pruning and compact indexes, because sparse search is attractive only if the representation stays sparse enough for cheap matching. More broadly, it echoes many 2026 retrieval papers that ask whether a powerful model's internal knowledge is being expressed in a form that the downstream search procedure can actually use.
1018.ww: The method should work because it attacks the mismatch at the place where the mismatch is created. A learned sparse retriever does not only need a strong language model; it needs a usable output alphabet. If that alphabet contains many redundant spellings and case variants, the model has to divide limited learning and activation capacity across forms that should have supported one another. Coarse-graining gives repeated evidence a shared place to accumulate, so the model can spend more capacity on meaningful distinctions. Preserving the pretrained geometry matters because modern encoders already know many useful relationships among words and contexts. If transfer kept the normalized vocabulary but destroyed those relationships, the model would be simpler but less knowledgeable. Calibration matters for the sparse constraint. Sparse retrieval fails if important terms never activate, and it also fails if everything activates because then the fast lexical structure is lost. The paper's reported results are consistent with this story: ModernBERT improves on BEIR after transfer, failing models such as RoBERTa-large are resuscitated, and the abstract says the effect generalizes across architectures and domains.
1018.po: The payoff is a practical bridge between modern encoders and learned sparse retrieval. The abstract reports that Vocabulary Transfer lets ModernBERT reach 52.4 nDCG on BEIR, a 4.7 point improvement, and that it revives failing models such as RoBERTa-large. That means the lag is framed as a vocabulary mismatch rather than an architectural defect. If the claim holds, teams do not have to choose between older encoders that happen to fit sparse retrieval and newer encoders that work better elsewhere. They can migrate advanced models into a sparse-friendly vocabulary at minimal computational cost and keep the CPU-friendly, term-based advantages of sparse search.
1018.limits: The argument depends on the coarse vocabulary preserving meaning. If normalization merges terms that users or documents need to keep apart, the same compression that tightens learning can erase important distinctions. The abstract reports benchmark gains and broad effectiveness, but it does not prove that every domain has safe morphological groupings or that every language benefits from the same vocabulary design. The method also assumes the pretrained geometry is worth preserving and can be transferred faithfully. Activation calibration addresses dead outputs and dense collapse, but the abstract does not specify all settings where calibration might fail. Finally, the reported evidence is grounded in retrieval benchmarks and named architectures, not in a long-running deployed search system with changing queries and documents.

1019.bp: Online stores, video apps, and content platforms do not learn preference from one kind of action. A person may view an item, favorite it, put it in a cart, and only sometimes buy it. Each action says something different: viewing is weak interest, favoriting is stronger, carting is close to intent, and purchase is the final target many systems care about. Multi-behavior recommendation uses these related traces so the system is not forced to learn only from rare final actions. The paper asks what happens when this richer setting meets a real production fact: interaction data does not arrive as one finished table. It arrives continuously. New behavior edges keep appearing between users and items. A system trained once on an offline snapshot becomes stale, but rebuilding the whole model each time is expensive. This paper serves the practical need to keep recommendations current while preserving the useful preference structure learned from older, heterogeneous behavior records.
1019.wh: The difficulty is a three-way pressure between freshness, cost, and memory. If the model ignores new events, it misses changed interests and new evidence. If it fully retrains whenever new events arrive, it spends too much computation and time. If it merely adjusts itself on the newest data, it can suffer catastrophic forgetting, meaning the new examples overwrite older preference knowledge that is still useful. The multi-behavior setting adds another layer. Views, favorites, cart additions, and purchases are not interchangeable copies of the same signal. They have different strengths and a rough behavioral order: a person often views before buying, but not every view should be treated as a near-purchase. Existing incremental recommendation methods mostly assume one behavior type, so they cannot use these relations among actions. The hard part is updating a connected user-item map over time while keeping both old neighborhood information and the different meanings of behavior types intact.
1019.naive: A smart beginner might keep one recommendation graph where users connect to items and simply append every new interaction as it arrives. Then the model could be fine-tuned on the fresh edges, saving the cost of full retraining. This is attractive because it treats streaming data as a small update rather than a complete rebuild. It fails in two ways. First, mixing all behaviors into one edge type loses the difference between browsing, favoriting, carting, and buying, so weak and strong signals blur together. Second, training mostly on new events can pull the model away from older patterns, especially for users or items not well represented in the latest stream. The result may be quick, but it can forget stable interests and misunderstand how earlier behaviors lead toward the target behavior.
1019.ap: The central move is to make incremental updating aware of behavior type instead of treating the stream as a single pile of clicks. The proposed BIGCN-MTL model has one part that updates the user-item graph incrementally while preserving old neighborhood information and behavior cascading dependency. In plain terms, it keeps track of both who interacted with what and which kind of action happened, so new evidence can be folded into the old map without erasing it. The second part, historical interest distillation, asks the updated model to stay consistent with older preference knowledge where that knowledge should remain stable. It uses non-interest consistency and preference comparison across old and new signals to reduce behavioral semantic forgetting. Multi-task learning means the model learns from several behavior prediction tasks together, so each behavior type contributes evidence while still keeping its distinct role.
1019.mech: The input is a stream of user-item interactions, where each event has a user, an item, and a behavior type such as view, favorite, add-to-cart, or purchase. The system starts from a model already trained on earlier interactions. As new data arrives, the behavior-aware incremental graph convolution part updates the connected map rather than rebuilding it from scratch. A graph here is a set of users and items joined by interaction links. A graph convolution is a repeated neighborhood update: a user representation is revised using connected item evidence, and an item representation is revised using connected user evidence. The paper's version is behavior-aware, so the message carried by a view is not treated as identical to the message carried by a purchase. It is also cascading, so the model can preserve the dependency among behavior stages, such as weaker actions helping explain stronger ones. After this graph update, the multi-task part learns across behavior-specific objectives instead of optimizing only for one target event. Historical interest distillation then compares the new model's preference signals with historically learned signals. Non-interest consistency discourages the model from suddenly treating previously uninteresting items as meaningful without evidence. Preference comparison keeps stable user interests close enough to their earlier form. The output is an updated recommender that scores items while using both the new stream and the older multi-behavior structure.
1019.math: The main mathematical object is a changing graph. Users and items are the nodes, and actions are typed links between them. The reason a graph fits is that preference evidence is relational: an item means more when we know which users touched it, and a user history means more when we know which items and behavior types connect it. The graph update spreads information across these links, but with separate meanings for different behaviors. That is a way of averaging and weighting nearby evidence without pretending every neighbor says the same thing. The second idea is learning from several related tasks at once. Each behavior type gives a training signal, and the shared model must find settings that serve them together. This matters because purchases are sparse, while views and favorites are more common but weaker. The third idea is distillation, which means using an older model's outputs as a memory target for the newer model. Instead of trusting only the latest data, the updated model is penalized when it drifts away from stable historical interests. The tradeoff is plasticity versus stability: the model must change enough to absorb the stream, but not so much that old preference structure and behavior meanings collapse.
1019.dots: This paper sits at the crossing of recommendation, graph reasoning, sequential behavior, and efficient learning. It connects to ranking because the final system still has to order candidate items for a user; the method improves the evidence behind that order rather than merely changing the sorter. It connects to network methods because user-item links are treated as roads along which preference evidence can travel, with the important warning that different road types carry different messages. It also connects to sequence and continual-learning work because the input is not a frozen dataset but a stream where new examples arrive after the model has already learned. Within recommender-system papers, it belongs beside work on long histories, preference drift, calibration, and incremental updates: all ask how a system can remain useful when user behavior changes over time. Its distinct angle is that freshness must be solved together with multi-behavior evidence, not after simplifying behavior into a single click or purchase label.
1019.ww: The approach should improve over the naive update because it protects the structure that makes multi-behavior data valuable. A purchase may be rare, so a model trained only on purchases has little evidence for many users and items. Views, favorites, and cart additions fill in earlier signs of interest, but only if the model keeps their meanings separate. Behavior-aware graph updating lets new events modify the neighborhood map while respecting those distinctions. The cascading dependency helps because behavior types are often ordered by commitment: earlier actions can support later ones, but they should not be read as identical to them. Historical interest distillation adds a memory brake. When fine-tuning would let recent examples dominate, distillation asks whether the new model is unnecessarily changing stable preferences or behavior meanings. Multi-task learning also gives the shared representation repeated pressure from several related prediction problems, which can make sparse target behavior less brittle. The intuitive reason is simple: the model listens to the new stream, but it keeps asking whether the new evidence truly changes what was learned before.
1019.po: The payoff is a recommender built for streaming multi-behavior data rather than for a clean offline snapshot. According to the abstract, BIGCN-MTL improves recommendation performance and training efficiency compared with full retraining on four real-world datasets. Practically, that means the system aims to refresh recommendations as new views, favorites, cart additions, and purchases arrive, without paying the full cost of rebuilding the model every time. It also buys a more faithful use of weak and strong behavior signals, so sparse final actions like purchases can be supported by richer surrounding evidence. The paper contributes the IMBR problem setting as well as a proposed solution.
1019.limits: The claims depend on the recorded behavior types genuinely reflecting preference stages. If views are accidental, favorites are used inconsistently, or cart additions mean different things across users, behavior-aware learning can preserve misleading distinctions. The graph assumption can also fail when connected users and items are not actually informative neighbors, or when popular items dominate many neighborhoods. The abstract reports four real-world datasets, but it does not specify from this input how broad the domains are, how severe the streams are, or how the method behaves under sudden large preference shifts. The approach also assumes old preference knowledge should often remain stable; that can be wrong when users deliberately change interests.
